0.title: In the Beginning, and What Went Wrong
0.essay:
The first three chapters of the Bible answer the deepest questions human beings ask. Where did everything come from? Who are we? Why is the world so beautiful, and yet so broken? Why do we die? Is there any hope?

Genesis answers

A good and all-powerful God created everything from nothing. He made human beings in his own image, male and female, to know him, love him and rule his world under him. But the first man and woman rebelled, and sin and death entered the world. Every page of Scripture that follows is the story of how God sets out to undo the damage — and it begins with a promise in Genesis 3:15.

Debated chapters

These chapters are also among the most debated in the Bible. How long were the days of creation? Was Adam a real man? How does Genesis relate to modern science? This study sets out the main views fairly and then gives a verdict. But its main aim is not to win arguments. It is to help us worship the Creator, understand ourselves and see our need of the Saviour.

The chapters

In the Beginning, God — the Creator and his good world. Six Days — how to read the days of Genesis 1. Made in God’s Image — the dignity and calling of every human being. Adam: The First Man — why his history matters for the gospel. The Fall — what went wrong, and how it affects us all. The First Gospel — the promise of a coming deliverer, and its fulfilment in Christ.

1.title: In the Beginning, God
1.essay:
“In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). The Bible’s first sentence is its foundation. Before anything existed, God was. He did not need the world; he created it freely.

Out of nothing, by his word

God did not shape material that already existed, as an artist works with clay. He spoke, and things came to be. “By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible” (Hebrews 11:3). It is the first example of faith in the great chapter on faith, because everything else depends on it. “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made… For he spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood firm” (Psalm 33:6, 9). Creation is a reason for awe: “Let all the earth fear the LORD” (Psalm 33:8).

The work of the Trinity

The Father created through the Son, the eternal Word, by the Spirit. “All things were made through him” (John 1:3). “For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible… all things were created through him and for him. And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:16–17). And at the very beginning, “the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters” (Genesis 1:2). Creation was made by Christ and for Christ, and it continues only because he sustains it.

Good and ordered

Again and again in Genesis 1, God saw that what he had made was good. At the end, “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). The physical world is not evil or unimportant. Matter, bodies, food, beauty and work are God’s good gifts.

The chapter also shows God bringing order out of formlessness. The earth begins “without form and void”. On the first three days God forms realms — light and darkness, sky and sea, land and plants. On the next three he fills them — sun, moon and stars; birds and fish; animals and humanity. The world is not random. It reflects the mind of a wise Creator.

For his glory

“The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork” (Psalm 19:1). Creation exists to display God’s power, wisdom and goodness. That is what gives everything — and everyone — meaning.

Creator and creature

The most basic distinction in reality is between God and everything else. Creation is not part of God, as pantheism teaches, nor independent of God, as deism imagines; it depends on him every moment.

The difference from the stories of Israel’s neighbours is striking. Their creation myths were full of warring gods, with the world made from a dead god’s body and humans made as slaves to feed the gods. Genesis tells of one God, no struggle, a good world, and human beings made with dignity in his image.

Because God made an ordered world and made us able to understand it, science is possible and good. Christians need not fear honest science. But Scripture, not changing theories, is our final authority about origins.

Seeing the world rightly

When Paul preached in Athens to philosophers who worshipped many gods, he began with creation: “The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man” (Acts 17:24). The doctrine of creation was his starting point for the gospel.

A teenager was told at school that the universe is an accident and human life has no meaning. Reading Genesis 1 and Psalm 19 with his father, he began to see the world differently. The stars were not meaningless; they declared God’s glory. And he was not an accident; he was made by God and for God.

For reflection

What does it mean that God created “out of nothing”? How does the goodness of creation shape your view of the physical world and your body? When you look at the natural world, do you see an accident or the handiwork of God?

2.title: Six Days
2.essay:
Genesis 1 describes creation in six days, followed by a seventh day of rest. How should we read those days? Since the rise of modern geology and evolutionary theory, it has become one of the most debated questions in the church. Faithful Christians who love the Bible hold different views. It is not a test of salvation — but it matters.

What the text says

Each day is marked by the words “And there was evening and there was morning”, followed by a number: the first day, the second day, and so on. When God had seen that everything was very good, the sixth day ended (Genesis 1:31). Then “on the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done. So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy” (Genesis 2:2–3). The rhythm of six days of work and one of rest begins in God’s own work.

Later, the fourth commandment grounds Israel’s week in that creation week: “Six days you shall labor, and do all your work… For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day” (Exodus 20:9, 11). The argument assumes that God’s days and Israel’s days correspond. Every Sabbath in Israel pointed back to the beginning.

Mature from the start

God made Adam as a grown man, not an infant, and trees already bearing fruit. A creation made in six days would have been functional and mature from the beginning. And Jesus, answering a question about divorce, went back to creation: “from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female’” (Mark 10:6). He treats Genesis 1 and 2 as real history, and places humanity at the beginning of creation, not at the end of billions of years.

Death before the fall?

Scripture links death to sin: “sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin” (Romans 5:12). The whole creation “was subjected to futility” and waits to “be set free from its bondage to corruption” (Romans 8:20–21) — a brokenness Paul ties to the fall, and which will be undone. Many Christians believe this rules out long ages of animal death, disease and suffering before Adam’s sin, when God had called his creation very good.

The views

The day-age view reads each day as a long age, matching the scientific timescale. The framework view sees the days as a literary structure arranging creation by topic rather than chronology. The analogical view sees them as God’s work-days, like ours but not identical in length. Theistic evolution holds that God created through evolution over billions of years, often treating Adam as a representative figure rather than the first man. The six-day view holds that God created in six ordinary days.

The verdict

The six-day reading is the most faithful to the text. The days are numbered and marked by evening and morning. Exodus 20:11 grounds the human week on God’s week. Jesus and Paul treat Adam as a real first man at the beginning of creation. And the link between sin and death fits a creation without death before the fall. The other views are held by godly Christians, but they arise largely from pressure outside the text. Scripture, not the changing scientific consensus, should govern our reading.

And on every view held by orthodox Christians, certain things are non-negotiable: God is Creator; creation is good; humanity is made in his image; sin entered through the fall. Hold your convictions firmly and humbly, and treat those who differ as brothers and sisters.

Faith and science

A university student studying biology felt torn between her faith and her lectures. She met an older Christian scientist who held the six-day view. He did not mock her questions or pretend they were easy. He helped her see that Scripture is her final authority, that science has limits when it speaks of unrepeatable past events, and that many questions remain open. She left with her faith strengthened and her mind still curious. Do you let Scripture shape how you read science, or science shape how you read Scripture?

For reflection

What are the main views on the days of Genesis 1, and what are the strengths of each? Why does Exodus 20:11 matter for how we read Genesis 1? How can Christians who disagree on this question show charity to one another?

3.title: Made in God’s Image
3.essay:
“Then God said, ‘Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over the livestock and over all the earth’” (Genesis 1:26). Of everything God made, only human beings bear his image. Our identity and our purpose come from him.

What the image means

Scripture does not give a simple definition, but it shows several things. We are made to know God and relate to him. We have reason, moral awareness, creativity and the capacity for love. We are made to rule creation as God’s representatives — like the statues ancient kings set up to show where their rule extended. And we are made male and female, in relationship. Both men and women bear the image equally; their differences are part of God’s good design, not a barrier to equality.

God “formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7). We are not souls trapped in bodies, nor merely bodies. We are unified persons, body and soul.

Small, but crowned

Looking at the night sky, David marvelled: “When I look at your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have set in place, what is man that you are mindful of him…? Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor” (Psalm 8:3–5). Hebrews applies the psalm to Christ, the true man who fulfils humanity’s calling (Hebrews 2:6–9).

Dignity

Every human being bears God’s image: rich and poor, young and old, born and unborn, healthy and disabled, of every nation and race. This is the foundation of human dignity and human rights. It is why murder is so serious: “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image” (Genesis 9:6). It is why even cursing someone is wrong (James 3:9). And since God “made from one man every nation of mankind” (Acts 17:26), racism is a denial of the doctrine of creation. There is one human race.

A nurse in a care home looks after elderly residents with dementia. Some cannot speak or recognise anyone. She treats each one with gentleness and respect, because she sees in them the image of God. Her colleagues notice the difference.

Dominion as stewardship

God gave humanity a task: “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion” (Genesis 1:28). This is not permission to exploit, but a calling to care for and develop the world as God’s stewards. Adam was put in the garden “to work it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Work, science, art and culture are all part of that calling.

Marred, and restored

After the fall, the image remains (Genesis 9:6; James 3:9), but it is defaced. We still have dignity, but our minds, hearts and wills are corrupted by sin. And in Christ it is restored. Christ is “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15). Believers “have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator” (Colossians 3:9–10). In this new humanity ethnic and social divisions no longer define us: “Christ is all, and in all” (Colossians 3:11). God’s purpose is that we be “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29).

For reflection

What does it mean to you that you are made in God’s image? Is there a group of people you find it hard to see as bearing God’s image, and what would change if you did? What does dominion over creation mean — and what does it not mean?

4.title: Adam: The First Man
4.essay:
Genesis 2 zooms in on the creation of the first man and woman. God shaped the man personally and gave him life by his own breath. What happened to Adam matters for all of us — and so does the question of whether he really lived.

In the garden

“Then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature” (Genesis 2:7). God planted a garden in Eden full of beautiful and fruitful trees, including the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Humanity began in intimacy with God, in a place of beauty and provision.

God put the man in the garden to work it and keep it, and gave him generous freedom, with one prohibition: “of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die” (Genesis 2:17). The test was simple: would Adam trust God’s word? Everything that follows hangs on his response.

God saw that it was not good for the man to be alone. He made the woman from the man’s side and brought her to him, and Adam’s joy was immediate. Marriage began as God’s gift.

A real man

The rest of Scripture treats Adam as a historical person. Genesis 5 lists his descendants and his age. Luke traces Jesus’ genealogy back to “Adam, the son of God” (Luke 3:38). Jesus treated the creation of the first couple as history (Matthew 19:4–6). Paul told the Athenians that God “made from one man every nation of mankind” (Acts 17:26).

Some Christians, often influenced by evolutionary science, see Adam as a symbol of humanity, or as one representative chosen from a larger population. The historic Christian view is that Adam and Eve were real individuals, specially created by God, from whom all humanity descends. The historic view is right — and the gospel itself depends on it.

Two Adams

Paul builds his teaching on sin and salvation on a comparison between Adam and Christ. “Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned… For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:12, 19). Adam’s one trespass led to condemnation for all; Christ’s one act of righteousness leads to justification and life. And the gift is far greater than the trespass: “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

“For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:21–22). The two Adams stand at the head of two humanities. If there was no first Adam, Paul’s argument about the second loses its foundation.

Our representative

Reformed theology describes Adam as the covenant head of humanity. God dealt with him as our representative, so his fall became ours. That can seem unfair. But the same principle is what allows Christ to represent us and save us. If we refuse to be represented by Adam, we cannot be represented by Christ. (The Covenant Theology study explains this further.)

A Christian read that many scholars consider Adam a myth and wondered whether it mattered. Studying Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15, he saw that the whole gospel is built on two men, Adam and Christ. If one is a myth, what about the other? He became convinced that Adam’s history matters.

For reflection

Why does it matter that Adam was a real historical person? Read Romans 5:12–21 and list the contrasts between Adam and Christ. How does Christ, the second Adam, succeed where the first Adam failed?

5.title: The Fall
5.essay:
Genesis 3 is one of the saddest chapters in the Bible. It explains why the world is the way it is — why there is shame, conflict, toil, disease and death — and why our own hearts are bent away from God.

The temptation

The serpent began by questioning God’s word: “Did God actually say, ‘You shall not eat of any tree in the garden’?” (Genesis 3:1). Then he denied God’s warning: “You will not surely die.” Then he slandered God’s motives, suggesting God was holding back something good (Genesis 3:4–5). The woman “saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise”; she took and ate, “and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate” (Genesis 3:6).

The serpent’s strategy is still the same: question God’s word, deny its warnings, slander his goodness. And the same three steps follow in us: we look, we desire, we take.

Shame and hiding

Their eyes were opened, but not as they had hoped. They knew they were naked and felt shame. Sin promises knowledge and freedom and delivers shame and separation. When God came walking in the garden, they hid. He called, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9) — not because he did not know, but to draw them out. Adam blamed the woman, and by implication God who gave her; the woman blamed the serpent. Fellowship with God was broken, and so was trust between them.

The curse

God pronounced judgment. The serpent was cursed. The woman would bear children in pain, and conflict would mark her relationship with her husband. The ground was cursed because of Adam, so that work would become toil. And death would come: “for you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). Finally they were driven out of the garden, away from the tree of life. Yet even in judgment, God did not destroy them immediately. He let them live, and the story continued.

The effects on us all

Adam’s sin was not only his own. “Sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned” (Romans 5:12). This is what Christians call original sin, and it means two things. First, Adam’s guilt is counted to all humanity, because he was our representative. Second, every person inherits a corrupt nature, inclined toward sin from birth: “Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity” (Psalm 51:5). We are not sinners because we sin; we sin because we are sinners.

Paul describes humanity’s natural state: “dead in the trespasses and sins”, following the world and the devil, living in the passions of the flesh, “by nature children of wrath” (Ephesians 2:1–3). This is what Reformed theology calls total depravity. It does not mean people are as bad as they could be. It means sin has affected every part of us — mind, will, emotions and body — and that we cannot save ourselves.

Sin grows. In Genesis 4, Cain murdered his brother Abel out of jealousy. By Genesis 6, “every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually” (Genesis 6:5). And the fall affected all creation. Disease, disaster, decay and death are symptoms of a world under the curse. Relationships, societies and nature itself are bent out of shape.

Why did God allow it?

Scripture does not fully answer this. But it shows that God was not taken by surprise. Christ was the Lamb “foreknown before the foundation of the world” (1 Peter 1:20). God permitted the fall in order to display his grace, justice and glory in a way that would not otherwise have been seen.

“But God”

A Christian watching the news felt overwhelmed by violence, injustice and suffering. Reading Genesis 3, he understood that this is not how the world was meant to be. The brokenness is real, and it has a cause. But Genesis 3 also contains a promise, and that gave him hope. Paul’s grim description in Ephesians 2 is followed at once by two great words: “But God, being rich in mercy…” (Ephesians 2:4).

For reflection

How did the serpent tempt the woman, and how does temptation still work this way? Where do you see the effects of the fall in your own heart today? Read Ephesians 2:1–10: how does “But God” change everything?

6.title: The First Gospel
6.essay:
In the middle of the curse, God gave a promise. Speaking to the serpent, he said, “I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel” (Genesis 3:15). It has been called the first gospel — the first announcement of the good news.

A coming deliverer

God promised that the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent’s head. There would be conflict, and the deliverer would be wounded — but a heel wound is not fatal, and a head wound is. Victory was promised, at a cost. Notice too that God spoke this promise before he pronounced the curses on the man and the woman. Grace was spoken first.

Genesis 3:15 sets up a conflict that runs through the whole Bible: the offspring of the woman against the offspring of the serpent. It is seen in Cain and Abel, in Israel and the nations, and finally in Christ and Satan. The Old Testament traces the line of promise through Seth, Noah, Abraham, Judah and David.

When Eve gave birth to her first son, she said, “I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD” (Genesis 4:1). Perhaps she hoped he was the promised deliverer. He was not; he became a murderer. The promise would wait thousands of years.

Fulfilled in Christ

Jesus is the offspring of the woman, born of Mary. At the cross the serpent struck his heel: Christ died. But by that death he crushed the serpent’s head, “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). Paul ends Romans with an echo of Genesis 3:15: “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). The victory Christ won will be shared by his people. The war that began in Eden will end in triumph.

Clothed by God

After the fall, Adam named his wife Eve, “because she was the mother of all living” (Genesis 3:20) — an act of faith in God’s promise of life. Adam and Eve had tried to cover themselves with fig leaves. But “the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them” (Genesis 3:21). An animal died so that their shame could be covered. It is a picture of what God would do in Christ: clothing sinners in his righteousness. Then he sent them out of the garden, guarding the way to the tree of life. Judgment and mercy were woven together.

Paradise restored

At the end of the Bible, the tree of life reappears, by the river of the water of life, in the new Jerusalem. “No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face” (Revelation 22:3–4). The story ends where it began, with a garden — but now a city filled with the redeemed. What was lost in Eden is restored, and more.

A new creation now

That restoration has already begun. “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come” (2 Corinthians 5:17). The God who said “Let light shine out of darkness” has shone in our hearts “to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). Salvation is a new act of creation. The Bible’s storyline moves from creation through the fall to redemption in Christ and the new creation; the Big Story of the Bible study traces it in full.

A woman who had made a mess of her life felt her story was beyond repair. A friend showed her Genesis 3:15 and 21, and 2 Corinthians 5:17. Even in the garden, God had a plan of grace. She realised that the God who promised to crush the serpent could make her new.

For reflection

Why is Genesis 3:15 called the first gospel? How did Christ fulfil the promise of crushing the serpent’s head? What does God clothing Adam and Eve teach about salvation? Could you explain Genesis 3:15 to someone else?
